o: Count permutations of 0..n-1 where certain prefixes contain exactly specified inversion counts. Key fact: inserting the i-th smallest element into a permutation of the previous i-1 elements adds anywhere from 0 to i-1 new inversions, and every permutation arises uniquely this way. Requirements pin down the inversion count at particular prefix lengths; between pinned points all counts flow freely.
k: dp[i][j] = number of permutations of the first i elements with exactly j inversions.
Inserting the i-th element adds t inversions for any t in [0, i-1], giving a sliding-window sum transition.
At a required end index e with count c, keep only dp[e][c] and zero the rest.

a.i: Build permutations incrementally. dp[i][j] = sum of dp[i-1][j-t] for t = 0..i-1, since the newly inserted element can create any number of new inversions in that range. After finishing prefix length i, if a requirement targets end index i-1, mask the DP so only the required count survives. The answer is the surviving mass at i = n. With n <= 300 and counts <= 400 the triple loop is fast enough.
s: Map requirements into a dict req[end] = cnt; let maxj = req[n-1].
For i = 1..n compute nd[j] = sum of dp[j-t], t in [0, min(i-1, j)].
If i-1 is a required end, zero nd except at the required count; return dp[maxj] at the end.
a.t: O(n · maxj · n) ≈ O(n² · maxj) — about 4.8e7 operations for the given limits
a.sp: O(maxj) for the rolling DP array

a.i: The inner sum over t is a sliding window of width i over the previous DP row. Maintaining a running prefix sum reduces each row update to O(maxj), yielding O(n · maxj) overall — important if limits were tighter.
s: For each row, accumulate pre += dp[j], and subtract dp[j-i] once j >= i.
Assign nd[j] = pre; apply requirement masking as before.
a.t: O(n · maxj) — sliding-window sums replace the inner convolution loop
a.sp: O(maxj) for the rolling DP array

w: The guarantee that some requirement has end = n-1 means the final answer is a single masked entry. Watch modular subtraction (add MOD before reducing) and the possibility of an infeasible requirement count (return 0). A follow-up: reconstruct one valid permutation by walking the DP backwards.
